content.thinking:
I need to write this whole module in one pass without verification, so I should be careful about API correctness upfront. I'm picturing a koala clinging to a eucalyptus branch stand in pixel art - a vertical trunk on a base with a forked branch, sized roughly to a real koala's sitting height.

I'm planning out the scene: a wood plinth base, a tapering trunk rising vertically at the back, and a horizontal branch jutting forward where the koala sits with its bum on the branch and legs wrapping around it in a relaxed, neutral pose with limbs separated.

I'll go with a horizontal branch along X at y=0.45, with the koala sitting in the fork, legs straddling it. For the stand itself: a wooden plinth base, a vertical trunk rising to about y=1.15 with a radius of 0.075, and the main branch extending out with leaf clusters on top.

For the koala pose: hips rest on the branch near the trunk with legs wrapping around to grip it from both sides, while the arms reach forward and down to hold the branch in front, hands placed just beside it. I'll add a smaller upward branch near the head for additional leaves to frame the scene.

I'm sizing the koala as a seated stylized figure roughly 0.55m tall with a chunky oversized head, placing the branch curving slightly upward from the trunk, and setting overall model height around 1.5m including the leaf canopy.

Now I'm working out the skeleton: hips at the base, a short spine rising through chest and neck to a large round head barely separated by neck, with torso about 0.4m tall and the head roughly 0.26m across, plus big round ears sized around 0.1m.

I'll build the spine as a 4-span catmull chain through 5 points, naming the joints spine1 through neck, then attach the head as a separate joint parented to the last spine joint so it can have its own jaw articulation rather than just following the path tangent.

Now I'm working out the torso geometry — sweeping a pear-shaped body profile along the spine chain using a radius function to define its silhouette.

That gives a fine texel density, so 0.02 cell size works for fur. I'm planning the fur shading using a grey ramp tied to the surface normal, with a cream patch on the chest where the normal faces forward, and keeping the overall flat color palette minimal since paints and textures don't count toward the limit.

I'm settling on a blue-grey fur ramp with a separate cream ramp for the chest, pink inner ears with white fringes, a big black nose, and tiny dark pixel eyes with highlights. For the head shape I'm weighing boxy primitives with cellPaint-based fur texture against a rounded sweep form to get a softer, rounded head silhouette.

Rather than fight the joint's tilted local axes, I'll just place parts directly in model coordinates using world-aligned boxes attached to the head bone, since the head has no pose rotation. For the jaw hinge, I'll set it as a child joint of head, offset and aimed forward with a default roll.

Now I'm sketching the actual head geometry: a wide, flattish box for the skull, a protruding rounded nose box near the top-front using a small pixel-art texture for shading and highlight, and I'm starting to work out the muzzle dimensions beneath it.

Designing eye pixel texture...

Now I'm planning the koala's ears — big round fluffy shapes on the sides, built as extruded disc outlines facing forward with a stepped circular profile for the fuzzy edge.

Figuring out the ear placement and inner pink paint region relative to each ear's center using local coordinates...

I'll skip the fringe cards and just add a cream disc behind the ear for simplicity. For the body, I'm sweeping a tube along the spine chain with front-facing normals getting cream chest coloring and dithered edges, keeping the ellipse symmetric regardless of orientation.

I'm working out the body's radii at different points along its length to get that bulgy seated shape, tapering from wider hips down near the branch up to a narrower neck, and positioning the branch so the bum sinks slightly into it for a natural seated look.

For the geometry, I'm deciding on faceted (non-smooth) circular cross-sections to keep that chunky pixel-art aesthetic rather than smooth shading. Then I'm placing the arms so they reach forward and down from the shoulders to grip the branch, with hand positions set on either side of the branch's top surface.

I'm working out the paw geometry with a wrapping grip around the branch, and checking that the two-segment arm length (upper arm plus forearm) can actually span the distance from shoulder to hand, bending the elbow outward and down accordingly.

So the three points are root, elbow, and wrist, with the final name being the hand bone at the tip, parented to the chest joint and offset so the shoulder sits away from center. I'm checking the limb function's signature to confirm it takes root, target, lengths, and bends as arrays, then planning to sweep a tapered radius along the arm chain for skinning and apply the same fur coat before moving on to the hands.

Now I'm working out the hand geometry: a small dark palm box at the wrist, three finger rods and two opposable thumb rods with claws, positioned to curl around the thin branch. I'm figuring out exactly how to place the hand relative to the branch's centerline and orientation so the fingers appear to wrap naturally around its grip point.

I'm considering placing the two hands at slightly offset positions along the branch to avoid finger collisions, weighing an asymmetric layout against a simpler symmetric one for rigging ease. I settle on having the palm sit atop the branch with fingers draping down each side in a chain from palm to fingertip.

Computing finger wrap angles...

I'm worried about finger/thumb positions colliding between the two hands, so I'll simplify: each hand gets 3 wrapping fingers plus a thumb kept on its own near side behind them, avoiding symmetric z-overlaps.

Setting up 4-digit chains per hand with auto-generated joint names and two spans each, keeping the total joint count within limits and parenting each digit chain to the wrist.

I'm also working out where the wrist target should sit relative to the palm box and branch surface so fingers rest naturally on top rather than floating or clipping through it.

Checking left and right palm placement to confirm they don't overlap near the branch center, then positioning the finger arcs so they originate from the palm surface with proper depth spacing between fingers and thumb along the z-axis.

I'm working out the branch's curved path using control points and tapering its radius from a thicker trunk end down to a thinner grip point near where the hand wraps around it.

I'll let the body sink slightly into the branch since the overlap is small enough to look natural. For the legs, I'm working out how the koala straddles the branch—hips angled outward, knees bending out and down, with feet gripping the branch from the side as if wrapping toes underneath for a believable perch.

I should cap toe wrap angle at 150° to keep both feet's digits from overlapping at the bottom. Checking the leg geometry, the hip-to-ankle distance is about 0.21 while the limb segments total 0.34, so the knee needs a significant outward-forward-up bend, which actually matches a koala's natural knee posture.

Setting the leg tube radii thicker near the hip to match koala thigh bulk, and treating the gripping rest pose as acceptable since the brief calls for a gripping stance. For the feet, I'm planning a dark sole pad plus digit chains—using four clawed toes rather than modeling true koala syndactyly, since that detail can be simplified.

For digit tips I'm adding tiny cream claw spikes oriented along the chain's tip frame, and sweeping each digit with a tapered dark-skin cross-section. Koalas have no visible tail, so I'll skip that feature entirely.

Now I'm planning the display stand: a layered plinth with a darker beveled lower slab and lighter upper slab, possibly with a wood-plank texture and label plate. I need a root joint for the stand that stays fixed at the floor, separate from the hips joint so the stand doesn't move with the koala's rig.

Defining the joint hierarchy...

Settling on hips as the root parent with the spine chain branching off it. For the trunk, I'm planning a eucalyptus-style sweep with peeling bark texture—pale greenish-grey base with tan and red-brown patches, faceted sides, tapering radius, and vertical noise-based streaks for the bark pattern.

I'll stretch noise vertically for elongated bark texture, then build a ramp from creamy-grey to darker tones with salmon patches mimicking eucalyptus smooth gum bark. Then I'm mapping out the trunk path geometry, running from the base up to around 1.6m where it forks into branches above the koala.

Trimming the proportions down slightly so trunk and leaves stay balanced against the plinth, with the trunk topping out near 1.45m and foliage reaching 1.6m. I'm designing the eucalyptus leaves as hanging pixel-art cards, sickle-shaped with a blue-green palette and lighter midribs, hand-stamping the leaf texture...

Now I'm working out how the leaf card should orient once attached at the branch point, accounting for the 180-degree lean so the leaf hangs downward with its root at the top and tip pointing down, while still drawing the shape as if standing upright with root at bottom and tip at top before the flip is applied.

I'm sizing the leaf cards for eucalyptus proportions, roughly 0.15m long by 0.02m wide, picking a near-square pixel grid around 6x18 or 0.05x0.17 for the card dimensions so texels stay close to square, then defining a half-width function along the leaf's length that starts narrow at the petiole, widens around 35-40% up, and tapers back to a point at the tip.

Still working out the width formula...

For the leaf textures I'll want two tint variants, green-blue and olive, picked randomly, plus thin twig rods sweeping out from the branches to hold the leaf frames.

I'm figuring out the frame placement for leaves along twigs, binding them to the root bone since there are no explicit bones for the rods, and planning how the eucalyptus branch curves upward at its tip with leaves clustered near the end.

Now I'm placing hanging leaf twigs near the koala's face and branch, positioning a few curving outward to the sides so they sit beside the body without blocking the view, plus fanning out several crown twigs from the top of the trunk with hanging leaves, aiming for roughly eight leaves per twig for a sparse but natural look.

Scaling that up to around a dozen twigs and a hundred leaves total, keeping triangle cost low. I'm also adding a second forked branch off the trunk, one going up-right and one up-left, each with their own leaf clusters, plus thin slanted bark-peel strips scattered across the trunk surface for texture variation.

I'm designing the plinth with layered wood-textured boxes for base and top slab, then adding grass tufts, stones, and a small bronze plaque with pixel leaf art on the front face.

Working through plank orientation across the different faces, I realize a single row-index formula based on cell v-coordinate handles top and sides consistently. I decide to go with a tiled wood texture for the plinth and add moss as separate small boxes on top, though I need to reconcile the texel size mismatch between the fur cells and tile texture.

Settling on 0.02 texel for fur, bark, and wood, with a half-size 0.01 texel for fine details like eyes, noses, and leaf cards. I work through the plank proportions at this scale and decide the plinth should use the half texel too, then start sizing the wood tile texture to fit the plinth face dimensions.

Planning the plank layout with staggered joints and grain dithering, then starting to define the wood color palette for the pixel art.

Finishing the hash function, then planning wood grain streaks and plank tone variation using the hash, plus adding small moss tuft boxes at the trunk base and corners for texture.

I'm also adding a few grey stone boxes, flat leaf cards lying on the plinth top, and fuzzy cream pixel tufts scattered around the koala's ears, cheeks, and chin for fur detail.

Rather than piling on more boxes for head fur, I'm switching to stepped zigzag extrusions along the cheeks to form fringe-like fluff, mirrored on both sides, with columns of varying heights creating a hanging cream fringe below the ears.

Still adjusting fringe spans...

I'm sketching out the head geometry more precisely now: cranium box dimensions and position relative to center C, plus a rounded top piece sitting above it to shape the skull.

Now I'm building the facial features — a protruding cream muzzle box, a prominent black nose sitting on top of it, a grey nose bridge between the eyes, and starting the lower jaw box underneath.

I'm considering adding a small dark mouth line as a separate plane on the muzzle front, trying a simple curved shape to suggest a smile without overcomplicating the geometry.

Designing nostril pixel patterns...

I'll decide the nose can simply stay solid dark rather than add nostril dents, and plan to decal-paint the front faces as planes over the box geometry. Next I'm positioning the koala's small eyes on the face front, centered near the top of the muzzle area.

Adding a darker eyepatch plane slightly behind each eye for depth, then layering the eye itself a hair closer to the camera so they read as distinct features without clipping. I'll skip eyebrows, and shift to painting cream-colored fur around the muzzle and cheeks using a conditional coat tint based on position.

Now I'm working out ear placement — positioning them on the upper sides of the head with enough width and height to read as round koala ears, considering whether to tilt them slightly outward for a more natural forward-facing look, and setting their thickness so they sit just in front of the head's back surface.

I'm setting the ear position and sizing, then defining the painting logic for the ear rings using radial distance thresholds for inner pink versus cream fringe fur, plus body details like chest paint, leg fur, paw palm skin tone, and bone-colored claws before writing out the fur color palette array.

Still writing coat shader logic...

Still writing fur shader logic...

Finalizing the tuft pixel pattern...

I'm also thinking about scattering tufts onto the cranium box, filtering by surface normal so fur only appears on upper-facing areas of the head.

Now I'm confirming the sweep works with surface scatter and setting a downward flow vector for the cards so they drape naturally over flattened top surfaces. I'm also tallying up the total joint count across spine, head, arms, legs, and digits, landing around 55 joints.

I'm adding ear joints as hinges under the head, assigning explicit bones to body parts like ears and jaw, and now laying out the spine chain path coordinates rising from the hips upward.

Defining body radius profile...

I'm checking proportions against a real koala: the neck stays short, the head reads wider than the neck, and the skirt-like body width at the hips is a bit chunky but acceptable. I'm positioning the arms so they root inside the body near the shoulder, tracing a path down to the wrist with a short, tapered length.

Now I'm working out the leg chain, rooting the hip joints inside the body's hip radius and bending the knee outward so the thigh reads naturally, keeping everything parented correctly to the hips.

For the ankle, I'm computing where the foot lands along the branch curve using the catmull-rom interpolation at that z position, then matching the branch's tapering radius there so the foot sits properly on the surface rather than floating or clipping through it.

Now I'm placing the finger points wrapping around the branch at several angles, then spacing out the toes along the foot box and planning finger positions along the hand's z-range near the palm center.

Checking the wrist position relative to the palm, the geometry fits under the branch top fine. Computing the arm reach distance to the wrist target, it comes out under the fully-extended length, so the elbow needs to bend outward rather than the arm stretching straight.

Now I'm setting up the arm and hand bone hierarchy, attaching each hand to its wrist joint, and defining the finger digit chains with distinct names per side using a smooth curve through the knuckle points.

For finger shape I'm sweeping each digit with a narrow tapered radius, rounding the ends, and adding a small spike at the tip to form a claw. I'm deciding on coloring: dark sparsely-furred skin for the fingers and claws, with the palm using the coat color so it reads as furred on the back of the hand, and now I'm moving on to sweeping the leg chains with a thicker tapered radius profile.

Still shaping trunk path...

Now I'm adding a branch emerging from the trunk around y=0.52, giving it a gentle curving path outward with tapering radius toward the tip.

I'm checking that the branch radius and position line up with where the koala's hips and body would sit, so the bottom of the body ellipsoid naturally nestles into and slightly hides the branch.

Now I'm sketching a small twig sprouting up from the branch end, curving forward with a sparse leaf cluster positioned so it doesn't block the view of the koala's hands, plus some bark knot details and a cut cap at the twig's tip.

Defining the twigs array...

With lean around 150-155 the leaves hang at an angle rather than straight down, with flow controlling the swing direction and a slight bend for curl; I'm also enabling cross for two card planes so leaves read from any viewing angle, sized small with no tint. I want some texture variety between two leaf types, and I'm considering adding small gumnut capsules clustered on the twigs for extra eucalyptus detail.

I'm placing roughly ten tiny brown boxes with caps along the twig frames as gumnuts. Tallying parts total, I'm estimating around 400 across head, body, limbs, digits, claws, stand, and twigs, which feels manageable, and I'm listing out the texture set needed for eyes, patches, nose, mouth, leaves, and tufts.

I'm now settling on the flat color palette for each material—claws, skin, nuts, twigs, moss variants, stone tones, brass, and the plinth—while noting that textured parts carry their own colors independent of the part's assigned color.

For the fur coat, I'm applying it across the body, limbs, and head geometry using box-based UV painting, keeping in mind each box face has flat axis-aligned normals. I'm also shaping the head silhouette with a cranium box and wider cheek boxes extending outward to create the characteristic wide-at-the-bottom look.

Now I'm adding greyish-white cheek pads with a separate cream paint function that uses dithering and noise for texture, defining a cream color ramp from darker tan to near-white tones to shade the forehead and top of the head.

I'm double-checking my imports to make sure everything I bring in from the pixel kit and math/path utilities actually gets used somewhere in the build, so the type checker won't complain about unused names.

Now I'm setting up metadata for the piece and defining pixel snapping constants and color helpers, then building the eye texture as a small pixel-art pattern with dark and white pixels to give it a shiny look.

Building eyepatch and leaf textures...

Now I'm figuring out the leaf texel sizing, then moving to building a wood plank tile texture with horizontal board lines and seam offsets per row.

Finishing the plank shading with tone variation and a noise-based color picker, plus placing small dark nail dots at fixed spots along each plank. Then I'm setting plinth dimensions—a lower and upper block with specific widths, heights, and vertical centers.

Now I'm applying the tiled wood texture to these boxes with a fixed plank alignment step, checking that the UV fit scales correctly against the texture size. I'm positioning the trunk to start right above the upper slab, then adding scattered moss and rock boxes on the plinth, and placing a small brass plaque box against the front face of the lower slab.

Designing plaque pixel texture...

Now I'm placing scattered fallen leaf cards on the plinth top, using leaning frame geometry with randomized flow, size, and mirroring to make them look naturally strewn about.

For the trunk bark, I'm defining a cell-painted texture palette with earthy bark tones and a salmon accent, sizing the cell resolution to the trunk's circumference so the pixelated look wraps cleanly, letting normals quantize to give it that chunky pixel-art feel.

The paint function layers two noise fields -- one stretched vertically for bark streaks and one patchier one -- so most of the trunk uses the bark palette with streak-based shading, but occasional patches shift into the salmon tones, plus random dark scar marks scattered sparsely. Branches reuse the same bark paint, and twigs get a flat brown color.

Now I'm laying out the foliage twigs as absolute coordinate paths forming the crown shape, defining each twig as a sequence of points curving outward and upward from the trunk.

I'm continuing to place twig branch paths, including side fork limbs, branch-end twigs near the base, and a couple of hanging lower twigs with drooping leaf points, then checking that the twig heights near the head roughly line up with where the ears should sit.

For the twig sweeps I'm generating tapered sweep geometry along each catmull-rom curve with small radii and a flat-to-round cap, colored with the twig material, and bone-attached to the trunk stand. Then I'm setting up leaf placement by sampling points along each twig path at increasing parameter values and building orientation frames for them.

Now I'm defining the card placement for leaves, using a golden-angle-based flow direction function and configuring size, lean, bend, spin, and sink parameters so the leaves hang outward and downward realistically from the twigs. Gumnuts just need small boxes sampled near the twig tips, and next I'm starting on the koala's fur tufts.

For the body I'm scattering tufts across a filtered surface sweep, using the body's coat paint as the tint so the cream chest color carries through naturally; limb tufts reuse surface scatters on the arm and leg sweeps, and head tufts scatter across the crown and cheeks with the same coat tint before moving on to placing the eyes as plane geometry parts.

Now I'm designing the ears with a stepped extrusion profile, and sketching a second cream-colored disc ring with slightly larger row widths to form an outer rim, shifting its vertical origin down by one row to keep it centered against the main ear shape.

For painting the ears, I'm writing a function that measures distance from the ear's center and uses it to blend an inner pink/rose "EARIN" color near the center, a cream color at the rim, and fur color elsewhere, with dithering for a natural blend.

Next I'm setting up the ear joints with hinge roles, positioning them relative to the head, and naming them earL/earR based on side. Then I'm working out the head's cranium geometry—placing a cranium box and a top chamfer box at specific coordinates to shape the skull with rounded proportions.

Still placing head details... cheek pads bulge slightly wider than the cranium with cream coloring, and I'm adding cheek fringe columns extruded along the z-axis beneath them for texture.

Now I'm positioning the jaw box beneath the muzzle, overlapping slightly so there's no visible gap, with a dark interior accent for mouth depth, and aligning a mouth plane on the muzzle front sized to fit the 8x4 texture grid.

I check the nose and bridge geometry for overlaps, confirming the nose plane is a touch wider than its box so I widen the nose to 0.08 to avoid floating edges, then position the eye sockets relative to the head's front face.

Now I'm setting up the limb naming and mirroring logic, using a loop over left/right sides so joints like shoulder, elbow, and wrist get consistent L/R suffixes, and working out the bend direction parameters for the limb function calls.

I'll keep the polyline as-is to preserve exact segment lengths rather than smoothing with catmull, then move to defining the arm sweep.

Still writing hand and finger geometry...

Still defining joint chains...

Computing toe arc points at angles 55/105/155 confirms they land within the foot box region. I'm also setting up the leg hierarchy naming for hip, knee, and ankle joints.

For the leg sweep, I'm tapering the radius from thigh to ankle for a chunky, rounded limb shape, and double-checking the spine chain has the right joint count and role assignment before aiming the head joint off the final spine joint.

Now I'm setting up the stand and hips joints, with hips branching into the spine chain and the two leg roots, making sure the parenting and roles stay consistent as I define the overall builder config for the koala.

I'm checking paint resolution against texture cell sizes — settling on paintSize 2048 so the atlas fits comfortably at 4096 without needing to downscale, and confirming the ears and body cells stay several texels wide. I'm also considering whether to add a belly bulge, rump pad, or cream-colored collar detail to the body.

For the trunk, I'm scattering bark-peel sticks across the sweep surface, using a flattened box shape with a slight y-filter so peels don't appear too low, and rotating through a few flat colors for variation. I'm also wondering if the koala's stand needs a small hanging tag detail.

Checking that leaf cards and tile-box parts correctly bind to the "stand" joint for rigid weighting, then moving to scatter moss tufts around the trunk base and corners with randomized box sizes and moss color choices, plus a small stack of grey stone boxes nearby.

I'm deciding to keep pure helper definitions (colors, functions) at module level while generating textures, paints, and randomized positions inside build() so repeated builds stay consistent, and double-checking the cellPaint pick signature and fur color ramp values.

Writing coat shading logic...

I realize this chest-cream zone overlaps with where arms attach, so I need to double-check the mask doesn't accidentally paint cream onto the arm geometry near those x and y ranges.

Knee patches should work fine too, and I'll add dithered speckles for texture plus ear fur detailing. Checking that noise function correctly accepts the Vector3 input, then I'll finalize the code and write a brief description, double-checking for any unused variables.

Designing tuft texture pixel art...

Now setting up the two leaf color palettes (dark, mid, light, tint variants) and starting a twig helper function for drawing branch points.

Adding gumnuts along the branch...

I'm defining a box helper for geometry, then working on the eye patches, positioning them symmetrically using a scale factor, and considering whether to mirror the highlight on each eye or keep it consistent on one side for simplicity.

Now I'm structuring the head surface with fur tufts collected into a parts array, checking the scatter filter logic against the hit normal, and verifying color typing is correct. I'm also checking plinth and branch clearances for the stand, assigning bones to card parts from each hit, and setting up the jaw joint with its parent, position, and aim.

I'm double-checking the limb and chain types for arm segments, then naming finger and toe joints across the sweep chains to make sure each generated name stays unique before writing it all out.
